title: Partitioning & Sharding
tagline: Split data across many machines to scale writes and storage — and avoid the hot-shard trap.
summary: Range vs hash sharding, the shard key, hot spots, rebalancing.

paragraphs: Replication scales *reads* (more copies), but every copy still holds *all* the data and every write still goes to one leader. When the dataset is too big for one machine, or write throughput exceeds one leader's capacity, you must **partition** (a.k.a. **shard**): split the data into pieces and put different pieces on different nodes. Now writes, storage, and total throughput scale horizontally.
Each shard is an independent database (and is itself usually replicated). The cost is a big jump in complexity — and it all hinges on one decision: the **shard key**.

blocks.caption: Each shard owns a slice of the keyspace; a router sends each request to the owning shard.

items.detail: Partition by key ranges (A–H, I–P, Q–Z; or by date). Pros: efficient range scans (e.g., 'all events in January'). Cons: easily creates hot spots — sequential keys (timestamps, auto-increment IDs) all land on the newest shard.
Apply a hash to the key and assign by hash range/modulo. Pros: spreads load evenly, no hot spots from sequential keys. Cons: kills range queries (adjacent keys scatter everywhere).
A lookup service maps each key (or key range) to a shard. Most flexible (move keys freely), but the directory is an extra component and potential bottleneck/SPOF.

rows: No range scans; rebalancing reshuffles a lot (use consistent hashing)

sections.title: Choosing the shard key (the whole ballgame)

paragraphs: A good shard key has **high cardinality** (many distinct values), **even access distribution** (no single value gets a huge share of traffic), and **aligns with your queries** (so most reads hit a single shard, not all of them). Choosing it well makes sharding invisible; choosing it badly creates hot shards and cross-shard queries that erase the benefit.

blocks.title: The hot-shard / celebrity problem
blocks.text: If you shard by user and one celebrity has 100M followers, that user's shard gets hammered while others idle. Mitigations: pick a higher-cardinality composite key, split hot keys into sub-keys, cache the hot entity aggressively, or special-case celebrities. Always raise hot spots — interviewers probe for it.

blocks.title: Cross-shard queries & transactions hurt
blocks.text: Queries that span shards (joins, 'top posts globally', multi-key transactions) require scatter-gather across nodes and lose ACID convenience. Design the shard key so the common queries stay single-shard; push the rare cross-shard analytics to a separate system.

paragraphs: When you add capacity, data must move to the new shard. Naive **hash mod N** is a disaster here: changing N from 4 to 5 remaps almost every key, forcing a massive reshuffle. The standard fix is **consistent hashing** (its own lesson), which moves only ~1/N of keys when a node is added/removed. Another approach is **fixed virtual partitions**: pre-create many more partitions than nodes and just reassign whole partitions to new nodes — cheap and simple to reason about.
Rebalancing should be incremental and online (throttled background copying) so it doesn't take the system down or saturate the network.

cheatsheet: Sharding splits data across nodes to scale writes + storage (replication only scales reads).
Range sharding → fast range scans but hot spots from sequential keys; hash sharding → even load but no range scans.
The shard key decides everything: want high cardinality, even access, and queries that hit a single shard.
Hot-shard/celebrity problem and cross-shard queries/transactions are the main pain points — always call them out.
Avoid hash-mod-N (reshuffles everything on resize); use consistent hashing or fixed virtual partitions to rebalance cheaply.
Each shard is itself replicated; rebalancing should be incremental and online.

questions.prompt: You shard a posts table by user_id. Most users are fine, but a few celebrities make some shards melt while others idle. What went wrong and what are your options?
questions.hint: Sharding by user concentrates all of a celebrity's load on one shard.
answer: Sharding by user_id puts *all* of a single user's data and traffic on one shard. For a celebrity with enormous read/write volume, that one shard becomes a hot spot — uneven load that sharding was supposed to prevent. The shard key has skewed access distribution.

Options, often combined: (1) **Cache** the hot entity's data aggressively so most reads never touch the shard. (2) **Sub-partition** hot keys — split a celebrity's posts across multiple sub-shards (e.g., key = user_id + bucket) and gather on read. (3) **Special-case** celebrities with a dedicated path (different storage/fan-out strategy). (4) Choose a higher-cardinality composite key if queries allow. The meta-point: detect skew, then break the hot key apart or serve it from cache.
keyPoints: Sharding by user concentrates a celebrity's load on one shard (skew)
Cache the hot entity to absorb reads
Sub-partition/split the hot key across shards, gather on read
followUps: How does this connect to the fan-out problem in a Twitter feed design?

questions.prompt: Why is sharding with `hash(key) % N` problematic when you add a new node, and what's the standard fix?
questions.hint: What happens to the mapping when N changes?
answer: With `hash(key) % N`, the shard for a key depends on N (the node count). Changing N from, say, 4 to 5 changes `% N` for almost every key, so nearly all data has to move to a different node at once — a massive, disruptive reshuffle that saturates the network and may require downtime.

The standard fix is **consistent hashing**: keys and nodes are placed on a hash ring, and each key belongs to the next node clockwise. Adding/removing a node only reassigns the keys between it and its neighbor — about 1/N of the data — instead of remapping everything. Virtual nodes smooth the distribution. (An alternative is pre-creating many fixed virtual partitions and moving whole partitions to new nodes.)
keyPoints: mod N ties mapping to node count → changing N remaps ~all keys
Consistent hashing moves only ~1/N keys on change
Virtual nodes for even distribution; or fixed virtual partitions
followUps: How do virtual nodes improve consistent hashing's balance?
